FADE IN:

INT. VETERAN'S BEDROOM - DAY

We see a small, cluttered bedroom. A WW1 veteran, JAMES (60s), lies in bed, his eyes closed. He's surrounded by old photographs, medals, and mementos from the war. A nurse, MRS. JENKINS, stands beside his bed, holding his hand.

MRS. JENKINS
James, can you hear me? Can you remember anything?

JAMES
(whispering)
No... nothing.

MRS. JENKINS
(softly)
It's okay, James. You're safe now. You're in 1953.

JAMES
(opening his eyes)
What year is it?

MRS. JENKINS
(smiling)
1953, James. You've been with us for a while now.

JAMES
(confused)
What... what happened?

MRS. JENKINS
(gently)
You were in the war, James. You fought for your country.

JAMES
(trying to remember)
I... I remember something. I remember looking to my side...

MRS. JENKINS
(encouragingly)
Yes, James. What do you remember?

JAMES
(hesitant)
I saw... I saw a man. He was shot in the head...

MRS. JENKINS
(concerned)
James, are you sure that's what you saw?

JAMES
(firmly)
Yes, I'm sure. His brains fell out from the back of his head.

MRS. JENKINS
(surprised)
James, that's not possible. You must have misremembered.

JAMES
(defensive)
No, I'm telling you what I saw. It's etched in my mind.

MRS. JENKINS
(gently)
James, it's okay. You're not alone. We're here for you.

James looks away, his eyes welling up with tears.

JAMES
(whispering)
I don't remember anything else. I don't remember my name, my family, my life before the war...

MRS. JENKINS
(softly)
We'll help you remember, James. We'll help you piece together your past.

James looks at Mrs. Jenkins, a glimmer of hope in his eyes.

JAMES
(determined)
I want to remember. I want to know who I am.

MRS. JENKINS
(smiling)
We'll get there, James. We'll get there.

FADE OUT.

* A WW1 veteran with dementia
* The veteran's attempts to remember things from the Great War
* The veteran's fragmented and disjointed memories
* The veteran's recall of a traumatic event, including the image of a man's brains falling out from the back of his head

The screenplay also incorporates elements of the reference text, such as the use of descriptive language and the focus on the veteran's emotional state. However, it also adds its own unique elements, such as the nurse's character and the veteran's determination to remember his past.
